p: Every day at 11am, a short Act of Remembrance and two-minute silence takes place at the arboretum. If you can, plan your arrival so you're there for it. Even on an ordinary weekday, when the whole site falls quiet, it's a powerful moment that many visitors say is the part they remember most.

The Armed Forces Memorial has its own clever piece of design. Gaps in its stone walls are lined up so that, at 11am on 11 November, a shaft of sunlight falls across the bronze wreath at its centre, weather permitting. Look for the names carved into the walls too: they record service personnel killed on duty since the end of the Second World War, and new names are still added.

Among the many other memorials, the Shot at Dawn memorial stops most people in their tracks. A blindfolded young soldier stands before rows of posts, each one bearing the name of a First World War soldier executed for offences such as desertion or cowardice, men who were later pardoned. It's a deeply affecting sight, and worth explaining gently to older children beforehand.

The site opened in 2001 and has grown hugely since. The Remembrance Centre near the entrance holds the exhibitions, café and shop, and is a good base to plan your route from. Allow at least half a day, and wear comfortable shoes.

Alrewas village itself sits on the Trent and Mersey Canal, a pretty spot for a towpath stroll. Lichfield, a short drive away, has more to offer than its cathedral, including the Samuel Johnson Birthplace Museum and Erasmus Darwin House.
